lessons.title: రాత్రి (rātri) — "night," this time matching the expected pattern
lessons.gloss: "night" — the same Sanskrit tatsama word already hiding inside ardharātri; unlike day's Persian surprise, night genuinely follows the Sanskrit-tatsama-as-everyday pattern, matching Kannada

segments.text: Last lesson's rōju broke every expectation. This one is more straightforward — but still worth checking honestly, not assuming.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - రాత్రి — Telugu's genuine everyday word

segments.text: రాత్రి (rātri) — "night" — is a Sanskrit tatsama word, already hiding inside అర్ధరాత్రి (ardharātri, "midnight," Chapter 17). Unlike rōju's Persian surprise, rātri really is Telugu's ordinary, everyday word for "night" — matching Kannada's own pattern this time, not breaking it.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - A messier story than Kannada's — three words, not one

segments.text: Telugu does have native words here — but be honest: it's a messier picture than Kannada's clean two-word story, not a tidy mirror of it.
రేయి (rēyi) — attested in older Telugu literature; most sources treat it as inherited Dravidian, though some grammars instead link it to rātri itself, so its native status is less than fully settled.
మాపు (māpu) — its primary sense is actually "evening, dusk" (as in రేపుమాపు, "morning and evening"), with "night" only a secondary, extended sense — not a clean synonym for rātri.
ఇరులు (irulu) — a genuine cognate of Kannada's ಇರುಳು (iruḷu), but its primary modern sense is "darkness," archaic even in that use.

All three have been effectively pushed aside by the Sanskrit loan — but unlike Kannada's single native competitor, Telugu's "native" side is split across three words in three different, overlapping senses.

segments.instruction: rēyi, māpu, irulu — three native words, three overlapping senses, all pushed aside
segments.source: [YOU SAY: rēyi, māpu, irulu — three native words, three overlapping senses, all pushed aside]

segments.text: Where have you already met రాత్రి before this lesson? (అర్ధరాత్రి, ardharātri, "midnight.") Does rātri follow the same "Sanskrit-as-everyday" pattern as Kannada's rātri, or does it break the pattern the way rōju did for "day"? (It matches — rātri really is Telugu's everyday word.) Does Telugu's native-word story cleanly mirror Kannada's single-word iruḷu? (No — it's messier: three words, రేయి/మాపు/ఇరులు, in three overlapping senses, not one clean replacement.)

lessons.title: జ (ja) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character జ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: జ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ణ — what does it do? And one from further back: ళ?
One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
జ — ja.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not j, it is ja.
You already say these, and every one of them has జ (ja) somewhere inside it:
రోజు rōju — day, the word that came in from Persian.
జ్యేష్ఠం Jyēṣṭhaṁ — the third of the twelve months.
ఆశ్వయుజం Āśvayujaṁ — the seventh.

Rōju is worth a second look. Its first letter is the ర you traced inside namaskāram. Its last is జు — this new letter carrying the u sign you met early on. The vowel sign in the middle is one this book has not stopped on yet, so the word is not wholly yours on the page. Two of its three pieces are, and that is new today.

blocks.title: Writing: జ — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on జ (ja) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
